title: Channel 4: complaints, programmes and financial pressures
label: 17 November 2026 · Channel 4's work and future
summary: Channel 4’s leaders discussed the handling of past complaints about Russell Brand and Married at First Sight, the steps they say they are taking to improve safety, and concerns about confidentiality agreements and industry-wide accountability. They also explained why Channel 4 cancelled Married at First Sight, outlined job cuts and plans for regional work, and defended partnerships to reach audiences on Disney+ while protecting Channel 4’s independence. Committee members welcomed some planned changes but pressed for stronger, more independent scrutiny and clearer evidence that complaints are handled well.

glossary.definition: The Creative Industries Independent Standards Authority, an organisation intended to improve behaviour and safety across the creative industries.
The UK regulator that oversees television, radio and other communications services.
A non-disclosure agreement, a contract that restricts what someone can share.
A legal agreement, often made when someone leaves a job, that sets out the terms for resolving a dispute.
A public-service broadcaster, which provides programmes intended to serve the public as well as attract audiences.
A UK news and television production company that makes Channel 4 News and programmes for other broadcasters.

chapters.title: Complaints and safety at work
chapters.takeaway: Channel 4 says it has improved its reporting systems, but the Chair questioned whether people who complained in the past were properly heard and whether an independent inquiry is needed.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Channel 4’s Dispatches investigation helped bring Russell Brand’s behaviour into public view. But a former employee, known as Bella, says her complaint about an assault in 2009 wasn’t properly investigated then or when she raised it again in 2023. Has Channel 4 done enough to protect people and investigate complaints made inside the organisation?

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: Bella’s complaint should have been investigated properly both times. The previous chief executive apologised, and that apology stands. We’ve strengthened Speak Up, our anonymous complaints service, and complaints are reported regularly to the board.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Bella says the later investigation was a shambles and that she had to repeat her account several times. She also knows of other people whose complaints were mishandled. How can former staff, not just current employees, be sure they won’t fall through the gaps?

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: I’m horrified to hear others may have been missed. Anyone in that position can contact Speak Up and remain anonymous. People also contact us through viewer enquiries or directly, and we should make sure they reach the right people without having to repeat painful experiences.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Bella says she was passed between people after calling the main switchboard. Having a system on paper isn’t enough if people don’t feel safe using it. Can you be certain staff have that confidence?

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: No, I can’t say that everyone feels confident. We believe Speak Up is strong and anonymous, but people may not trust it, so there should be other ways to raise concerns. We’re willing to have the service audited.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Would you commission an independent inquiry into what happened in 2009 and 2023?

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: A thorough review was conducted under the board’s ethics committee, with a large document review and interviews. It wasn’t independent: a member of our legal and compliance team carried it out. We’re now focused on improving how complaints and welfare are handled.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: That doesn’t give us confidence that people on Channel 4 productions will feel safe speaking up.

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: We can’t promise every person will feel confident, but we can make it clear that complaints will be taken seriously. We’re making CIISA registration mandatory for production companies we work with, and it could provide a neutral place to raise concerns.

turns.speaker: Alison Hume
turns.text: Young freelancers can be especially vulnerable, and a hotline on a call sheet may not be enough. Could they have a named person at Channel 4 to contact directly?

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: We’ve appointed a welfare executive, Cheryl Woodcock, so welfare complaints go to someone separate from the person responsible for commissioning the programme. We’ll make her role more visible if that helps people contact us directly.

turns.speaker: Alison Hume
turns.text: Channel 4’s supplier rules also cover disabled crew members and adjustments they may need. How do those rules work alongside CIISA’s standards?

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: Our supplier rules set out what companies and their staff should do, including making adjustments for disabled workers. They’re designed to work alongside CIISA’s standards, not replace them.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You’ve committed to requiring production companies to register with CIISA, but Channel 4 has only signed up for one year. Will you commit for three?

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: We’re committed to making registration mandatory for our production companies. Our own commitment is currently for one year because we have questions about the organisation’s plans for its second and third years, including how it would handle personal information and whether it could require people or companies to provide evidence.

chapters.title: Contracts, culture and prevention
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses rejected blanket gagging agreements and described culture changes, while members argued that systems and good intentions won’t by themselves prevent abuse or expose repeat offenders.

turns.speaker: Liz Jarvis
turns.text: Does Channel 4 use NDAs? A report described dozens of settlement deals with former employees and said £5 million was paid to keep complaints from escalating.

turns.speaker: Geoff Cooper
turns.text: A blanket NDA isn’t the right approach, though confidentiality terms can have a proper use in particular circumstances.

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: We don’t use blanket NDAs. Some employment contracts and settlement agreements have confidentiality clauses, but they shouldn’t prevent people reporting misconduct. Older agreements may have had broader wording; we’ve said we won’t enforce clauses that would stop someone speaking up.

turns.speaker: Liz Jarvis
turns.text: How many such agreements have been signed since 2021, and how many involved allegations of harassment or misconduct?

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: I don’t have those figures with me, so I’ll need to provide them later. Production companies make their own contracts with the people they hire; Channel 4 isn’t party to those agreements.

turns.speaker: Liz Jarvis
turns.text: Could a junior person on a set complain about a star without fearing for their job?

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: Their complaint should be taken seriously, but I can’t responsibly guarantee that every person will always get the response they deserve. My job is to set expectations, provide ways to report problems, and make clear that people who raise concerns shouldn’t suffer consequences for doing so.

turns.speaker: Liz Jarvis
turns.text: Did the money Channel 4 made from Big Brother affect how complaints about Brand’s behaviour were handled?

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: I wasn’t there, so I can’t say what people knew or why they made particular decisions. The review found no hard evidence that people at Channel 4 knew of the crimes Brand has since been convicted of. But commercial success can’t be allowed to override our values. I’ve walked away from a show when it didn’t fit those values.

turns.speaker: Geoff Cooper
turns.text: Commercial targets can affect how people respond to a complaint. The board is treating culture as a serious issue. We’re considering how people’s conduct should affect their bonuses, and we’re adding board members with direct experience of production and commissioning.

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: Culture also depends on who we hire, what behaviour we reward and who gets promoted. We’re recruiting a new people chief with experience leading cultural change, and we expect production companies to follow the standards we set.

turns.speaker: Nigel Huddleston
turns.text: You can have procedures and still fail to prevent abuse. Do you keep a watchlist of people whose behaviour raises concern?

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: There are informal lists in the industry, but they raise serious concerns about accuracy and people’s privacy. We make checks, ask about people’s conduct on previous productions and use our judgment, but we aren’t an investigative body.

turns.speaker: Nigel Huddleston
turns.text: People may have heard rumours for years before a complaint is made. Could the industry share information to spot patterns earlier?

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: That might help, and CIISA could potentially identify patterns across the industry. But we’d need to work out how to do that accurately and lawfully. No single measure will solve this: we need checks before filming, ways to monitor welfare during production and safe ways to report problems.

turns.speaker: Dr Rupa Huq
turns.text: Channel 4 also relies on outside producers. ITN has faced allegations about how workplace complaints were handled, including claims that women were silenced. Do you know whether ITN has joined CIISA?

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: I don’t know whether it has. We expect our production partners to register with CIISA, and I’m aware of the ITN complaints, though ITN is handling them through its own human resources team. I’ll look into the concerns raised with the Committee.

chapters.title: Why Channel 4 cancelled Married at First Sight
chapters.takeaway: Channel 4 cancelled the popular reality show after reviews proposed changes its chief executive believed would fundamentally alter it, but the Chair challenged how fully earlier complaints had been examined.

turns.speaker: Mr Bayo Alaba
turns.text: Why did you decide to cancel Married at First Sight?

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: Soon after I took the job, I received serious allegations from BBC Panorama. I commissioned a review by law firm Clyde & Co into how the complaints had been handled, and asked television executive Lorraine Heggessey to recommend future safety standards.

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: The reviews said the set’s standards were high and that Channel 4 hadn’t breached Ofcom rules based on the evidence examined. But some proposed changes, including recording around the clock and locking rooms and bathrooms, would have made it a completely different show. I decided to stop making it and use the budget for new programmes.

turns.speaker: Mr Bayo Alaba
turns.text: Does cancelling it acknowledge that the show had inherent risks or that Channel 4 failed in its duty of care?

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: That wasn’t what I meant by saying we’d take a different creative route. The reviews didn’t say the programme itself was faulty, though they did suggest changes that could be useful elsewhere. For example, they suggested people should choose to live together rather than having to opt out.

turns.speaker: Mr Bayo Alaba
turns.text: How did the show serve the public, beyond entertainment?

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: It began as a social experiment: could people build relationships if experts matched them? Over time it became more of an entertainment show. Some viewers also watched discussions about behaviour and conflict, but I wouldn’t overstate that part.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: People who took part have complained to Channel 4 and the production company, CPL. How many complaints about sexual misconduct were made during the show’s run?

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: I don’t have the total number. The review focused on the specific cases raised by Panorama, rather than going through every series and episode. We believe the complaints we looked at were handled appropriately, but if others feel they weren’t, we’ll take that seriously.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The journalists said they had more cases than they could include in the programme. Why didn’t your review establish the total number of complaints?

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: The review’s purpose was to examine those specific cases, not conduct a wider count. Channel 4 and CPL should have records, and I’m concerned if other people have not been heard.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: It looks as if Channel 4 examines problems only once public attention makes them a reputational issue. Bella’s complaint was even filed under “Reputation”.

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: That label was a default used by the people handling calls, and it was wrong. It was hurtful and we should have had a better process. We commissioned the Married at First Sight review before knowing whether Panorama would be broadcast, and it examined around 30,000 documents.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Doesn’t labelling an abuse complaint as a reputation matter say something about the organisation’s culture?

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: It was an error, and the process has been changed. I don’t believe the label reflects the organisation’s culture, but I understand why it caused concern.

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: We’ll also apply useful recommendations to other programmes, review practices regularly and rotate people who’ve worked on a production for many years, so new eyes can spot problems.

chapters.title: Job cuts, regions and new talent
chapters.takeaway: Channel 4 says a 28% staff reduction is intended to protect programme spending and make the organisation financially sustainable, while promising to retain offices and work across the UK.

turns.speaker: Gill German
turns.text: You’ve announced cuts of 340 jobs, about 28% of staff. What will that mean for Channel 4’s offices and opportunities outside London?

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: We’d reached a point where 40 pence of every pound went on costs other than programmes, up from 30 pence. Cutting 340 roles is a difficult decision, but we need to be sustainable and protect the money spent on programmes. We designed the changes without favouring one location over another.

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: We’re still consulting, so I can’t yet say how roles will be distributed. Nobody will be asked to move, and we’ll keep a presence in our existing cities. Leeds is especially important for our digital news and social media work.

turns.speaker: Geoff Cooper
turns.text: Our commitment to the nations and regions hasn’t weakened. I made sure my first day was in Leeds and that we scheduled more board meetings outside London, partly to show the organisation isn’t centred only on the capital.

turns.speaker: Gill German
turns.text: Will you protect 4Skills, your scheme for giving people training and entry routes into television?

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: We’re proud of it. It created 51,000 opportunities in the past year, including apprenticeships and writing programmes. The budget was doubled to £10 million, but next year will be constrained and it may fall. We want to grow it again.

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: Regional work goes beyond the scheme. Recent programmes have been made in Wales, Northern Ireland, Yorkshire, Manchester and Liverpool, and we work with production companies across the UK.

turns.speaker: Geoff Cooper
turns.text: Reducing staff is only part of the savings. We’re reviewing how and where we spend, while trying to grow revenue. The aim is to give Channel 4 more room to make sustainable plans for the future.

turns.speaker: Dr Rupa Huq
turns.text: Will the job cuts mean more programmes are made in-house, rather than commissioned from outside companies?

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: That isn’t the purpose of the changes. We’re simplifying how commissioning decisions are made, and may work differently with some larger companies, but we still want to work with smaller producers. We intend to protect Channel 4’s creative character.

chapters.title: Streaming partnerships and independence
chapters.takeaway: Channel 4 hopes its Disney+ partnership will bring new viewers and revenue without replacing its own streaming service, and says its editorial independence would be non-negotiable in any closer relationship with another broadcaster.

turns.speaker: Jeff Smith
turns.text: What’s the main reason for putting Channel 4 programmes on Disney+, and how will you judge whether the deal works?

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: People watch programmes on many different platforms, so we want to reach them where they are. Disney+ will carry our scheduled channel and a selection of programmes to watch on demand. A few shows will appear on both services on the same day, which may help them reach a bigger audience.

turns.speaker: Jeff Smith
turns.text: How will you know whether you’re gaining viewers, rather than shifting them away from Channel 4?

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: Disney will report viewing data, and we’ll look at whether viewers then use Channel 4’s own service and whether people’s awareness of the brand improves. Our own service will remain the main home of Channel 4 programmes.

turns.speaker: Jeff Smith
turns.text: Some of your most popular shows could be valuable to Disney. Are you worried about losing viewers or advertising income?

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: We’ve kept back our biggest shows, including Bake Off. The selection was carefully chosen, the agreement is for a set period, and Disney pays us. I’m confident the deal will make money for Channel 4.

turns.speaker: Jeff Smith
turns.text: Did you check that Disney’s approach fits with Channel 4’s values?

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: Yes. I met senior Disney executives and made clear that our branding must be prominent, our own service must remain important and not all programmes would move to Disney+. I felt they understood our public-service role.

turns.speaker: Jo Stevens
turns.text: Could Channel 4 programmes also appear on the BBC’s iPlayer?

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: It’s an idea worth exploring, but iPlayer doesn’t currently carry advertising. We’d also need to agree how Channel 4 programmes would appear in searches and recommendations, and make sure the arrangement didn’t undermine our ability to earn money and invest in programmes.

turns.speaker: Jo Stevens
turns.text: What about suggestions that Channel 4 could merge with the BBC?

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: A merger with a much larger organisation could amount to a takeover. Channel 4’s editorial independence is a red line: without it, we wouldn’t be Channel 4. But we should explore practical partnerships, such as sharing costs or working together on advertising.

turns.speaker: Geoff Cooper
turns.text: The board supports Priya in exploring partnerships while protecting the things that make Channel 4 distinctive.

chapters.title: News, sport and Channel 4’s future
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses argued that Channel 4’s news and distinctive programming remain central to its public role, while acknowledging financial pressures and the need to work with other broadcasters.

turns.speaker: Tom Rutland
turns.text: If Sky and ITV combine, what could happen to ITN and, in turn, Channel 4 News?

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: Channel 4 News is made by ITN, and I’m proud of the work. ITN is unusual because it makes news for several different broadcasters. If ITV’s support changes, ITN might struggle to keep producing our news at the same cost, which could affect quality. We’ve raised our concerns with Ofcom and the Competition and Markets Authority.

turns.speaker: Tom Rutland
turns.text: How do you make sure young people get reliable news, and how do you know your social media work is reaching people beyond the audience you already have?

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: We make news explainers for TikTok and YouTube, including longer videos that explain big stories. We follow Ofcom’s standards even when they don’t require it. We survey viewers, but we don’t receive enough information from platforms to track exactly what people watch next.

turns.speaker: Nigel Huddleston
turns.text: Channel 4 has earned a strong reputation for Paralympics coverage. Will you keep investing in it despite the financial pressures?

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: We’re proud of the coverage and the audience grew compared with Beijing. We’re discussing the next rights and would like to remain the free-to-watch partner.

turns.speaker: Nigel Huddleston
turns.text: Would you work with the BBC on sports such as the Commonwealth Games, rather than competing in ways that push up prices?

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: We’d consider partnerships, especially for sports that need wider coverage. The timing and cost would have to work with our budget, but I wouldn’t rule it out.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What should people judge your leadership by?

turns.speaker: Priya Dogra
turns.text: By the quality and distinctiveness of our programmes, and by whether we manage money carefully enough to secure Channel 4’s long-term future. We’ve spent much of today on past failures, but the changes we’re making are meant to protect that future.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We’ll follow up on the information you’ve promised to provide. We’d also like you to keep us updated on whether Channel 4 can commit to CIISA for three years.
